title: 为什么 Xbox 的游戏机广告可能对游戏行业是件好事 | 观点
content:
Why Xbox's console ads could be a good thing for gaming | Opinion | GamesIndustry.biz

Virginie Chesnais is CMO at the ad tech analytics platform
Happydemics
.
Gamers have long been wary of in-game adverts, and not without reason. Ads in gaming have a mixed reputation, with redirects to different websites or apps, deceptive content, or impossible-to-find close buttons all being common frustrations.
A recent eMarketers study found that
52% of gamers would quit playing
if they encountered multiple disruptive ad features. Losing half your audience at the point of engaging them isn't a great strategy.
But ads don't have to be bad. Indeed, the same survey claimed that one in five gamers would play a title more frequently if in-game ads were of high quality.
So, with Xbox currently
testing out its new ad-supported game streaming service
and the
cost of playing steadily increasing
, high-quality ads may well find a happy home in gaming.
Why ads? Why now?
The case for providing some form of ads-for-games-type deal is more attractive than some may think, having been at least partially proven by linear media. As Netflix, Disney, and other streaming services have shown, there is money to be made by providing a consistent service while also offering ad-supported tiers. If Xbox's approach proves successful, it will not only retain paid customers through its subscription service, but it will also unlock a brand new, previously untapped revenue stream at a time when the brand
sorely needs it
.
"Ad-supported tiers can open up a new way for players to enter the gaming sector without having to fork out for large upfront purchases"
This matters because console gaming is becoming much more of a premium service. The prices of games, consoles, accessories and downloadable content are becoming harder and harder for people to justify, creating a barrier for the everyday gamer.
As Xbox itself said in its announcement, when done well, advertising can help lower the cost of access to gaming. We've already seen from mobile gaming that ad-supported tiers can open up a new way for players to enter the gaming sector without having to fork out for large upfront purchases.
Plus, it's important to remember that this is entirely optional. Players who don't want to watch ads can do so if they choose, albeit through a paid subscription fee. By providing a two-tier system, Xbox is hoping to retain its loyal base of fans while also making games more accessible to newcomers.
Although no survey data on the news exists right now, I'm willing to bet that the vast majority of gamers would be willing to watch a 30-second advert if it meant playing one of their favourite games or a brand new title for an hour. Xbox will almost certainly know that's true.
Ad-supported gaming: friend or foe?
Happydemics data for 285 in-game campaigns across the UK and North America show that in-game ads consistently outperform TV, social, and online ads for ad recall and attribution. The data indicate that in-game ads are much more likely to be remembered and be correctly attributed to the brands that showed them.
This is where Xbox's around-the-game approach – that is, adverts that sit outside the game environment, for example being shown before the game starts – gets interesting as part of a bigger picture. Our data show that around-the-game formats have a clear edge on ad recall and attribution when compared with intrinsic in-game placements.
Adverts shown before a game show advantages in terms of ad recall and attribution
This matters because even though we can remember certain ads popping up when we're watching TV or scrolling through social media feeds, this doesn't always mean that we're linking those ads to certain brands. Gaming, it seems, is in its own league in terms of this metric, which is probably the reason why Xbox and other companies such as EA are
increasingly looking into ad-based gaming
.
But it's important to remember that Xbox's ads aren't in-game – they're pre-game. In-game ad formats hold the advantage further down the funnel, outperforming on brand image uplift, consideration, interest, and ad likeability. Combining both pre-game and in-game adverts, with their respective advantages, might be the ideal for advertisers – but it would also risk more pushback from players.
"Gaming, it seems, is in its own league in terms of linking ads to brands"
Xbox has stated that the ads won't be intrusive, which is simple to understand. Ads that come before the games themselves will ensure they won't disrupt the immersive experience. It's an important factor for not just the players, but also the advertisers, as they would want to ensure their campaigns are part of the experience, not disrupting it.
On the ads themselves, Xbox will have to ensure they're relevant. No one likes seeing ads for cat food when they don't own a cat or for games that they've already completed. By making ads contextual and giving a reason to show them, Xbox can ensure players won't crash out at the sight of them, while giving brands the best platform to reach new audiences.
But Xbox is in uncharted territory here. First in regards to how players will react to adverts, and second in terms of whether the ads will earn the company enough revenue to see them become a long-term option.
X marks the spot
The exploration of ad-supported game streaming is a shrewd move by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, who has shown she is willing to take risks and try new things. But only time will tell if the strategy works as intended.
Our previous work in gaming ads has mostly been built on 'watch an ad, get an extra life'-type trade-offs. Xbox is asking players to watch an ad to reach a game they already own. Nothing in our data set tells us how that lands.
